Model 6: Skew-t Niche (Branco & Dey 2001)

Source: vignettes/model_skew_t.Rmd
model_skew_t.Rmd

1 Ecological Motivation

Some species have environmental tolerances that are not only asymmetric but also heavy-tailed: they can persist at extreme environmental values with higher probability than a Gaussian or skew-normal model would predict. This is common for generalist species or species at range edges where occasional extreme events (heat waves, droughts) are tolerated.

The skew-t model extends the skew-normal (Model 4) by adding a degrees-of-freedom parameter r>0r > 0 that controls tail heaviness:

  • As r→∞r \to \infty, the skew-t converges to the skew-normal.
  • For small rr (e.g. r=3r = 3–55), the tails are substantially heavier than Gaussian.

The distribution follows the noncentral skew-t (NCST) of Branco and Dey (2001).

2 Mathematical Specification

2.1 Density

The skew-t density is derived as a scale mixture of skew-normals:

T=μ+Xr/Y,X∼SNp(0,Σ,α),Y∼χr2. T = \mu + X\sqrt{r/Y}, \qquad X \sim \text{SN}_p(0, \Sigma, \alpha), \quad Y \sim \chi^2_r. \tag{1}

The resulting density at 𝐭\mathbf{t} is:

fT(𝐭)=C(r,Σ)(2A(𝐭))(p+r)/2I(𝐭), f_T(\mathbf{t}) = C(r,\Sigma)\;\left(\frac{2}{A(\mathbf{t})}\right)^{(p+r)/2}\;I(\mathbf{t}), \tag{2}

where:

A(𝐭)=1+q(𝐭)r,q(𝐭)=(𝐭−μ)⊤Σ−1(𝐭−μ), A(\mathbf{t}) = 1 + \frac{q(\mathbf{t})}{r}, \qquad q(\mathbf{t}) = (\mathbf{t}-\mu)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(\mathbf{t}-\mu), \tag{3}

z(𝐭)=∑k=1pαk(tk−μk)σk, z(\mathbf{t}) = \sum_{k=1}^{p}\frac{\alpha_k(t_k - \mu_k)}{\sigma_k}, \tag{4}

I(𝐭)=∫0∞u(p+r)/2−1e−uΦ(z(𝐭)2uA(𝐭)r)du, I(\mathbf{t}) = \int_0^\infty u^{(p+r)/2 - 1}\,e^{-u}\, \Phi\!\left(z(\mathbf{t})\sqrt{\frac{2u}{A(\mathbf{t})\,r}}\right)du, \tag{5}

and C(r,Σ)C(r,\Sigma) collects the normalisation constants.

2.2 The Integral I(𝐭)I(\mathbf{t})

The integral in Eq. (5) does not have a closed form for p>1p > 1 and must be evaluated numerically. The integrand has the form uae−uΦ(⋅)u^a\,e^{-u}\,\Phi(\cdot), where a=(p+r)/2−1a = (p+r)/2 - 1. The factor uae−uu^a e^{-u} is exactly the kernel of a Gamma distribution, which makes Gauss–Laguerre quadrature the natural choice:

I(𝐭)≈∑q=1QwquqaΦ(z(𝐭)2uqA(𝐭)r), I(\mathbf{t}) \approx \sum_{q=1}^{Q} w_q\;u_q^a\;\Phi\!\left(z(\mathbf{t})\sqrt{\frac{2u_q}{A(\mathbf{t})\,r}}\right), \tag{6}

where (uq,wq)q=1Q(u_q, w_q)_{q=1}^Q are the standard Gauss–Laguerre nodes and weights (i.e. the quadrature rule for ∫0∞e−ug(u)du\int_0^\infty e^{-u}\,g(u)\,du), and Q=32Q = 32 in the implementation.

2.3 Why Q=32Q = 32?

The choice Q=32Q = 32 was validated by parity tests against R’s stats::integrate(rel.tol = 1e-12) for p=2p = 2 and log⁡r∈[log⁡2,log⁡100]\log r \in [\log 2, \log 100]. For p=2p = 2, the quadrature error is below 10−1010^{-10} across the tested range. For higher dimensions (p≥3p \geq 3), the exponent aa increases and additional nodes may be needed; users should verify with the parity test suite.

2.4 Negative Log-Likelihood

−ℓ(θ)=n2log⁡|Σ|+np2log⁡r+nlog⁡Γ(r2)+p+r2∑i=1nlog⁡Ai−∑i=1nlog⁡Ii+penalty, -\ell(\theta) = \frac{n}{2}\log|\Sigma| + \frac{np}{2}\log r + n\,\log\Gamma\!\left(\frac{r}{2}\right) + \frac{p+r}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log A_i - \sum_{i=1}^{n}\log I_i + \text{penalty}, \tag{7}

where:

  • log⁡|Σ|=2∑klog⁡Lcov(k,k)\log|\Sigma| = 2\sum_k\log L_{\text{cov}}(k,k),
  • Ai=1+qi/rA_i = 1 + q_i/r,
  • IiI_i is evaluated via Eq. (6),
  • the penalty includes ridge terms on log⁡σ\log\sigma, α\alpha, and log⁡r\log r.

Note: the constants −(p/2+1)nlog⁡2-(p/2 + 1)\,n\log 2 and p2nlog⁡(2π)\frac{p}{2}\,n\log(2\pi) are dropped to match the convention in Models 1–4.

3 Parameterisation

The unconstrained parameter vector θ\theta has length 3p+p(p−1)/2+13p + p(p-1)/2 + 1:

θ=[μ⏟p,log⁡σ⏟p,vC-vine⏟p(p−1)/2,α⏟p,log⁡r⏟1]. \theta = \bigl[\underbrace{\mu}_{p},\; \underbrace{\log\sigma}_{p},\; \underbrace{v_{\text{C-vine}}}_{p(p-1)/2},\; \underbrace{\alpha}_{p},\; \underbrace{\log r}_{1}\bigr].

Block Length Constraint Meaning
μ\mu pp Unconstrained Niche centroid
log⁡σ\log\sigma pp σk>0\sigma_k > 0 Marginal standard deviations
vv p(p−1)/2p(p-1)/2 Unconstrained C-vine partial correlations
α\alpha pp Unconstrained Skewness parameters
log⁡r\log r 1 r>0r > 0 via exp\exp Degrees of freedom

The degrees-of-freedom parameter rr is stored as log⁡r\log r at position θ[3p+nv]\theta[3p + n_v] to enforce positivity.

4 Implementation Call Chain 

optimize_niche(likelihood = "skew_t")
  └─ niche_obj.cpp::create_niche_obj_ptr()
       └─ loglik_niche_math_skew_t_eigen()         [C++, lines 760–823]
            ├─ build_L_cov()                        [theta → mu, sigma, L_cov]
            ├─ alpha = Map(theta + 2*p + n_v, p)    [line 776]
            ├─ log_r = theta[3*p + n_v]; r = exp()  [lines 777–778]
            ├─ Mahalanobis q via forward solve       [lines 785–786]
            ├─ z_vec = skew_z(diff, sigma, alpha)    [line 789]
            ├─ log_det = 2 * sum log L_cov(k,k)     [lines 791–793]
            ├─ For each i:
            │    A_i = 1 + q_i/r                     [line 801]
            │    sum_log_A += log(A_i)               [line 802]
            │    sum_log_I += log_skew_t_integral()  [line 803]
            ├─ prior_penalty_value(has_alpha=true)   [lines 812–813]
            └─ neg_log = 0.5*n*log_det + 0.5*n*p*log_r
                         + n*lgamma(r/2)
                         + half_kpr*sum_log_A
                         - sum_log_I + penalty       [lines 814–819]

4.1 The Quadrature Engine (lines 725–752)

The function log_skew_t_integral(q, z, r, k) evaluates log⁡I\log I for a single point:

  1. Computes A=1+q/rA = 1 + q/r and the exponent a=(p+r)/2−1a = (p+r)/2 - 1 (lines 727–728).
  2. Loops over Q=32Q = 32 Gauss–Laguerre nodes (uq,wq)(u_q, w_q) (lines 733–744):
    • Argument to Φ\Phi: arg=z2uq/(Ar)\text{arg} = z\sqrt{2u_q/(Ar)} (line 740).
    • Log-term: log⁡wq+alog⁡uq+log⁡Φ(arg)\log w_q + a\log u_q + \log\Phi(\text{arg}) (line 742).
  3. Applies the max-shift logsumexp trick across all QQ terms (lines 746–751).

The nodes and weights are hard-coded as constexpr double arrays (kGLNodes, kGLWeights, lines 677–715), generated by numpy.polynomial.laguerre.laggauss(32).

4.2 R Entry Point 

optimize_niche(env_occ, likelihood = "skew_t",
               prior_log_sigma_lambda = 1.0,
               prior_alpha_lambda = 1.0)

6 When To Use

  • When the species may have heavy-tailed environmental tolerances (survives extreme conditions more than a Gaussian predicts).
  • As a model-selection candidate: compare AIC/BIC with "skew_normal" and "presence_only". If r̂>50\hat{r} > 50, the skew-t is not adding value over the skew-normal.
  • For species at range margins where extreme environmental events are ecologically relevant.

7 Limitations

  1. Computational cost. Each log-likelihood evaluation requires Q=32Q = 32Φ\Phi evaluations per data point, making this model approximately 32×32 \times slower than the skew-normal per evaluation.

  2. Quadrature accuracy for p≥3p \geq 3. The parity tests validate Q=32Q = 32 for p=2p = 2. For higher dimensions, the exponent a=(p+r)/2−1a = (p+r)/2 - 1 increases, potentially requiring more nodes. Users should run the parity test suite (test-loglik_math_cpp_parity.R) for their specific pp.

  3. No background correction. This is a presence-only model. For background-corrected skew-t, use "skew_t_weighted" (Model 7).

  4. Parameter identifiability. With 3p+p(p−1)/2+13p + p(p-1)/2 + 1 parameters, the model requires large nn. For p=2p = 2, this is 8 parameters; for p=5p = 5, it is 26 parameters.

References

Branco, M. D., and D. K. Dey. 2001. “A General Class of Multivariate Skew-Elliptical Distributions.” Journal of Multivariate Analysis 79 (1): 99–113. https://doi.org/10.1006/jmva.2000.1960.
